title: Citizenship
objective: After this level you can explain what citizenship means.
summary: Citizenship is a two-way bond with a state: allegiance for protection. Most people get it at birth by soil (jus soli) or blood (jus sanguinis); adults can naturalize.

cards.headline: You probably never applied for your first citizenship.
cards.body: If you hold one, a country's law may have settled it the day you were born, using one of two old rules: where you were born, or who your parents were. First, though: what exactly did you get?

cards.headline: A two-way deal
cards.body: Britannica defines citizenship as the relationship between an individual and a state to which the individual owes allegiance and in turn is entitled to its protection. Read that as a trade. You owe the state loyalty; the state owes you protection. Remember Level 9's state, with its territory, laws and means of enforcing them? Citizenship is your membership card for one.

items.label: Right of the soil (jus soli)
points: Born on the territory? You're a citizen, whoever your parents are
The basis in nearly every country in the Western Hemisphere

items.label: Right of blood (jus sanguinis)
points: Citizenship passes from a parent, wherever you're born
Japan: a child is Japanese if the father or mother is

mascot.line: Don't sweat the Latin. Soil or blood: where you were born, or who your parents were.

cards.fact: Adults can join too. Canada asks for 1,095 days first.
cards.context: Becoming a citizen by applying is called naturalization. Britannica lists the usual requirements: a period of residence, language skills and knowledge of the country. Canada's version is at least 1,095 days (3 years) physically in Canada within the last 5, plus a citizenship test for applicants aged 18 to 54. Citizenship by birth is luck. Naturalization is homework.

cards.headline: Citizenship: granted
learned: Citizenship: allegiance to a state, protection in return
Jus sanguinis: citizenship from a parent
Naturalization: Canada asks 1,095 days and a test

questions.prompt: Under the rule called jus soli, what makes a newborn a citizen?

options.label: A parent's citizenship, wherever the baby is born
options.rationale: That's jus sanguinis, the right of blood.

options.label: Being born on the country's territory
Passing a test on the country's history
options.rationale: Tests are for naturalization, not newborns.

options.label: Living in the country for three years
options.rationale: That's a naturalization rule, as in Canada.

questions.explanation: Jus soli, the right of the soil, grants citizenship to anyone born on a state's territory, whoever the parents are.

questions.prompt: An adult born and raised in Japan moves to Canada and wants Canadian citizenship. Which route fits?

options.label: Jus soli, since Canada uses birthplace
options.rationale: They weren't born in Canada, so birthplace doesn't help.

options.label: Jus sanguinis, through Japanese parents
options.rationale: That passes on Japanese citizenship, not Canadian.

options.label: Nothing: citizenship can only come at birth
options.rationale: Adults can become citizens by applying.

options.label: Naturalization: time in Canada, then a test

questions.explanation: Naturalization is citizenship by application. Canada asks for 1,095 days in the country within 5 years, plus a test for ages 18 to 54.

questions.prompt: Level 9 told nations apart from states. In Britannica's definition, citizenship is a relationship with which one?

options.label: A state, which owes its citizens protection
A nation, meaning a shared culture or language
options.rationale: A shared identity isn't what you owe allegiance to here.

options.label: A family, which passes on its name
options.rationale: Parents can pass on citizenship, but the bond is with the state.

options.label: A political party you choose to join

questions.explanation: Citizenship ties a person to a state: allegiance one way, protection the other.
